utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Kehoe, will you be the first one to cross-examine Mr. Albiston?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we have no questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions at this time. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will have a couple of questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have a couple of questions. Mr. Albiston, will now be cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Cermak -- for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Albiston.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your report - and I refer to paragraph 3.61 - you touched upon a subject in which you explain that, generally speaking, it is accepted that the prevention of crimes is a very important role of the police and that there is certain doubt about the segments of the police work that should have the priority in specific moments, whether it's the prevention of crime or the investigation of crime. So could you please elaborate a little bit between prevention of crime and detection of crime, from the police point of view?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, sir. From the civilian policing point of view, in most jurisdictions, the primary responsibility for the prevention of crime rests with the uniformed branch of the police service. A number of police forces have specialised officers who are described as crime prevention officers, but that's a very technical function. It has to do with providing advice to businesses, shopkeepers, private citizens on things such as door locks and security in the home and the office and so on. But, generally speaking, crime prevention is effected by uniformed patrols in areas of crime or in some countries, cities, by the use of CCTV cameras and other technical devices. The investigation of crime is, in many police forces, a separate issue and is dealt with by officers who have special training in criminal law and procedure in forensic science and in techniques of investigating crime to do with interviews with witnesses, interviews with suspects, and that sort of thing. Now, in most police forces, the senior officers have to try and decide what proportion of their resources, of personnel and money, to put into the different aspects of policing, because both are important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Now, continuing in the paragraph 3.62 of your report, you say that in the aftermath of Operation Storm there was a period of violence and fairly intense criminal activity, which was clearly distinct from organised and directed combat. So, in a situation like that, and considering the area that we are discussing and which is the subject of the indictment, in such a situation, as a consequence of a war conflict, the criminal activities intensified. So this is not the usual picture of the operation of the police system. And the police system, therefore, has to adjust to such a situation in one way or another. While studying the materials, what did you find out in view of this issue?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's exactly -- it is entirely right to say that, in general, after conflict, there is an opportunity for crime and crime frequently follows combat, and that in these particular circumstances the material which I read suggested that certainly happened in the Krajina area in the period after Operation Storm. What I was attempting to distinguish between in the paragraph to which you referred was a period when there was military activity by the Croatian armed forces designed to achieve the objectives of the state in relation to the Krajina, and when it was generally considered that that operation had concluded, but there is evidence from the documents that there was a significant amount of crime taking place in the area. From my reading of the documents, what appears to me to have been the response of the Croatian state to this problem could be looked at in two ways. Firstly, you could look at the anticipation of such problems by the state, and there were a number of documents to which I referred, particularly the documents such as the documents by Mr. Moric on the 3rd of August and another document produced by Major-General Lausic around about that date - I'm an afraid I'm not able to quote the court numbers - which show the preparations of the state from the point of view of dealing with the potential aftermath of the operation. Looking, then, to what happened after Operation Storm, the documents which I would cite as an indication of the response of the state would include a long series of documents about the employment of, what are called in translation, separate police units, which were a form of reinforcements to the police, some of them apparently quite young and inexperienced officers. I would cite the evidence of witnesses such as the police coordinators, who were additional officers sent to help re-establish civilian policing, and they comment on the difficulties of police moving into the area. And, of course, there are other commentaries in the documents before the Court which indicate that there were a large number of crimes, but the number of officers available to investigate those crimes did not significantly increase, which would put additional pressures on them. So these are the sorts of things which I think the court documents show about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I saw that you did your work in crisis areas in Northern Ireland and in Kosovo, in a situation relatively similar to the one that existed in the Sector South after the conclusion of the Operation Storm there was an increase in violence and so on. Could you draw any parallels from your own personal experience?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there certainly are parallels to be drawn. There is always a danger that we exaggerate the degree of similarity. But parallels, there certainly are. There was a conflict involving peoples with long-standing animosities in the Balkan matters as well as in Northern Ireland. History plays a great part in determining peoples' attitudes to each other. And I think that this plays out in the conflicts and in the attitudes to authority; the attitudes to policing; the belief amongst some people that policing is not a non-partisan upholding of the law, but, rather, the exercise of power by one group over another. These are sometimes realities and sometimes exceptions, and they produce difficulties. They can turn issues which should be about law and order and common sense into political issues, and I think some of these problems pertained in the areas of the Balkans where I worked, as they certainly do in Northern Ireland. Another parallel would be that criminals, and particularly organised crime and violent gangsters, will see the breakdown of ordinary law and order as a opportunity for them to impose their will to establish a power-base and to engage in crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We could see a similar situation in recent history also in the events following the Hurricane Katrina in the area of New Orleans or also during the civil unrest in Paris in 2005, when, after certain events, in one case it was a natural disaster, in the other one it was an incident, there was an explosion of crime and violence. Was the reaction of the police in these well organised environments in comparison to the reaction of the police that could you see, in the documents that you studied for the needs of this proceedings, can be compared or can any parallels be drawn between these two?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I don't think there is a foundation laid for this question, in particular, the events following Hurricane Katrina or the civil unrest in Paris in 2005 vis-a-vis this witness's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, apart from the issue raised by Ms. Gustafson, of course, until now we have not received that much evidence on what happened after Katrina. Of course, also --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I think it's a common knowledge, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I said apart from what Ms. Gustafson raised. These kind of comparisons, what are we aiming at? To see that after disasters, whether natural disasters, or after wars, that there is a problem? I mean, that is common knowledge as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So could you please focus your questions on what this witness with his experience could tell us and what he could add to what we find already in his report on the basis of his experience and his knowledge of other events. So that -- get -- if we get focussed on -- on additional -- I would say additional value, probative value.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will try to do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Albiston, my direct question is: What is the role of police in situations when there is an increase of crime or even an explosion of crime in certain areas regardless of the consequences, whether it was a natural disaster or a war conflict or some other kind of hostilities, what is the role of police in a situation of this kind, and what can you tell us about this on the basis of your personal experience and on the basis of the documents which you reviewed for the purpose of writing your report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the short answer to the first part of your question is that the function of the police is to restore and then to maintain civil law and order. In relation to the second part of your question, that's slightly more complex. In my experience, in these situations, there is an role for the military, and there is a role for the police. And those who have the political direction have to make a decision as to when the military should be in the lead, because the problems are such that only the resources of the military can deal with them, and when the police should be in the lead, because, in fact, the problem is now seen as mainly a problem of civil law and order, rather than a problem which is beyond the means of the civilian policing. In some countries, of course, there are police branches or branches with a police name, such as the gendarmerie nationale in France, which have policing skills and policing functions but actually come under the Ministry of Defence, rather than the Ministry of the Interior, because it is accepted that the sort of techniques which they used in some of their duties are more akin to military techniques than to what a British person would regard as normal civilian policing techniques. In Northern Ireland, the decision was taken 30 years ago that the police should lead and use the military in support where it was necessary. In Kosovo at the time that I was police commissioner, we had one area in which the military took the lead and the police assisted where they could, and four areas where the police took the lead and called on military assistance. And that was based on a judgement of the level of security threat and the nature of the crime. So it won't always be the same thing. In the situation which this Chamber is considering, there was a military campaign followed by crime. And at some stage it was the responsibility, I would suggest, of the Croatian government, to decide when the military campaign was concluded and when it was possible to establish normal civilian law and order through the means of the civilian police, investigating judges, and prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Albiston, while you were studying materials for the purpose of writing your reports, did you come across any proof, any document, that will allow to you conclude that when it came to the wish to establish law and order in the newly liberated territories, the Croatian government, by any of its measures or activities, that is to say the Ministry of the Interior or the Ministry of Defence, did they in any way obstruct this duty or this task? Did you come across any evidence that would point to the contrary, the wish not to re-establish civil law and order in the newly liberated territories? Did you ever come across any evidence that would point to anything of the kind?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. In fact, quite the contrary. The documents which I concentrated on, as my research developed, it became clear to me there were certain areas that I should concentrate on. And those areas, in particular, the documents to which I referred in examination-in-chief which show the efforts of Mr. Moric to establish civil law and order, there is nothing in any of those documents to suggest that the Croatian government was taking an obstructive or negative views towards its responsibilities. What there is is an indication of matters which I have seen in every jurisdiction in which have I worked which is that sometimes things don't work properly, sometimes people don't turn up to appointments. Sometimes you don't have the right number of people in the right place, despite what you have tried to achieve. I saw evidence of failings in that regard, but I didn't see any evidence of organised failings or obstruction by superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers, Mr. Albiston.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Albiston, if you would allow me one follow-up question in relation to one of your answers. You gave as one of the parallels that -- and you said that: "... criminals, and particularly organised crime and violent gangsters, will see the breakdown of ordinary law and order as an opportunity for them to impose their will to establish power-base and to engage in crime." That was the parallel through the other experiences compared to the situation in the Krajina. Could you tell us what actually you had on your mind when you said that organised crime and violent gangsters would see here an opportunity? What gangsters, what crime did you have in mind? What organised crime did you have in mind on the basis of the documents you have studied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well the reference to the organised and violent crime was more to the parallels to which counsel was talking about. And my personal experience of that is taking place in Kosovo and in Northern Ireland. The parallel from the documents is not entirely clear. There are indications in the documents of criminal activity and police officers and others being threatened. But I wouldn't try to suggest to this Chamber that I have identified particular individuals engaged in organised crime in this area. What I'm saying is that that is one of the opportunities which is presented by this sort of situation, one of the challenges with which the police might be expected to deal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then there must have been some misunderstanding as far as the question is concerned, because the question was introduced by Mr. Mikulicic, referring to your experience in Northern Ireland and Kosovo, and he then said: "In a situation relatively similar to the one that existed in the Sector South after the conclusion of the Operation Storm, there was an increase in violence and so on," whether you could draw any parallels. But I do understand now that as far as organised crime is concerned, and violent gangsters, that you are comparing more Kosovo and Northern Ireland but have you no clue for Sector South.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying that the same opportunities were there, but the documents don't show me that that took place in the period which we're discussing. The documents suggest violence but not of that particular type.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Ms. Gustafson, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston you will now be cross-examined by Ms. Gustafson. Ms. Gustafson is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Albiston.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I would like to start by asking you some questions about the methodology of your report, the sources you relied on, and the process that you undertook in producing it. And it's clear from your report and the supplemental note that you provided that you were initially briefed by Mr. Kay on the 15th of December, 2007. Prior to that briefing, had you ever -- did you know Mr. Kay, had you met anyone in the Cermak Defence or --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No. Do you know how the Cermak Defence came to contact you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the first stages of the contact process. The later stage of the contact process were that a former senior police officer who knew me and of my experience rang me and said that the Cermak Defence team were looking to take advice from a police expert and would I be interested, than's what the -- I said yes, if you want me to meet someone, then the meeting with Mr. Kay took place, as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you said the meeting that you had initially lasted approximately three hours and that Mr. Kay briefed you on the nature of the allegations, the nature of the Defence case. What specifically did Mr. Kay tell you about the Defence case, in relation to the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a very simple outline. The -- the main allegations against Mr. Cermak were outlined, and Mr. Kay told me that the Defence did not accept those allegations because they said that Mr. Cermak's role was rather different from what the Prosecution's allegation was. And the -- basically the line taken by Mr. Kay in his briefing to me was that the Defence case was that General Cermak's role was more to do with the restoration of normality in the Knin area and not so much to do with the events that were taking place around there. Certainly not the events that were outlined in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So did Mr. Kay tell you or did it otherwise become clear to you at that meeting that the position of the Cermak Defence was that General Cermak had no authority over the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that that came out of that meeting. We only had a short time. And most of the meeting was actually taken up by Mr. Kay trying to explain to me the -- the facts of what had happened in Operation Storm, as opposed to the details of the case. I mean, you know, a basic historical outline, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And were you, at that time, just asked to draft a report, or were you asked to be -- have some kind of consulting expert role or both?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was told that, if I agreed to become an expert witness for the Cermak Defence team, I would be expected to produce a written report which would be tendered to the Court, and I would be expected to produce that document in evidence to the Court, and to be challenged on the contents, if the Prosecution didn't agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And at paragraph 1.5 of your report, you describe the purpose of the report, and you say: "It would be to examine the evidence connecting General Cermak to policing issues and to offer expert opinion, based on professional experience, as to General Cermak's role and responsibilities as garrison commander in Knin in relation to policing. He was further invited to comment upon Croatian Ministry of Interior structures and any difficulties which might have faced the police at this time." Now, was that instruction given to you in written form or in oral form?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in oral form, to start with, although at one stage a note was produced saying basically what the terms of my engagement were.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And what I read out to you and what's in paragraph 1.5 of your report, does that reproduce exactly what the terms --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the language isn't exactly similar, but the substance is similar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in producing your report, were you, at any time, asked do assume any specific facts or any -- any specific evidence?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, yesterday, I think you said you estimated the number of documents you were provided to be between 2.000 and 4.000.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And there are, not having counted them exactly, but approximately 200 documents cited specifically referenced in your report. And I understand that it was the Cermak Defence who selected the documents to be provided to you. Do you have any idea how those documents were selected by the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them were selected by the Defence team because they were documents which they thought that I needed to see; and some of them were documents which I asked to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And which documents did you ask to see?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a long process which has been going on over 18 months. I'm not sure I can be entirely specific. I asked to see material which would demonstrate the workings of the criminal justice system in the area at the time, because I thought that the workings of the criminal justice system were relevant to my comments on civilian policing. I asked to see transcripts of the evidence of certain witnesses. I won't say who they were now, but I think they're well-known to this Chamber. By and large, everything that the Defence team saw that they thought might be relevant to me, I'm sure, was what was passed to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But you have no knowledge of the specific factual or evidentiary criteria that they applied in making that selection?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And aside from asking about -- asking for documents about the workings of the criminal justice system and asking to see the transcripts of the evidence of certain witnesses, did you ask for any other documents from the Defence, at any time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may -- I may have done, but I -- I can't recall. I'm trying to think of examples now. The ones that come to mind are the cases of the -- those witnesses which I thought were particularly germane to the area that I was covering.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say you had relatively frequent contact with the Defence about the documents that you were to look at?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly. It was made clear to me from the very start that anything that I asked for, the Defence would seek to provide for me so that I could consider it. It would be wrong for me to say that I went to some great archive and conducted my own research. I didn't. And if the suggestion is that the material that I got was material which was provided by the Defence, that would be entirely correct; it was Defence material. Of course, it's material which is -- material in the Chamber. There is only one example I can think of of a case where I asked for material and I was told I couldn't have it, and that was quite recently. I asked if I could see the expert report being prepared by General Deverell in relation to the military aspects of the Cermak Defence, and I was told it wouldn't be appropriate for me to see that. But everything else that I have asked to see, I have been shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And going back to something else you said yesterday, which was -- you said: "I tried to read most of the material that was provided to me." And that was at page 23.765. My question is: Were there any documents provided to you by the Cermak Defence that you did not read?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I read them all. Some of them had more of a lasting impression, and some of them were documents from which I jotted down notes as I believe that they were relevant to my area of expertise. There were, of course, particularly in the early stages, a significant number of documents which were useful for me to read in order to have a flavour of the background of the case and to see what people, at the time, thought was going on in the area. But, actually, when it came to me writing an expert report based on my expertise in relation to the matters which I could actually address with some credibility as an expert, that narrowed the ground down significantly. So there were lots and lots of documents that I read that won't feature in my report and that I -- I wouldn't comment on to the Chamber, because they're not matters that I feel that I can comment on expertly. I mean, a lot of them are documents which would be questions of evidence of fact for the Chamber and not matters upon which I, as an outsider, could usefully comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And just in relation to that, you were asked yesterday about the methodology used when selecting documents for your report. And that's when you gave your answer about trying to read all the material. And I'd just like to try to get a more specific answer from you about the criteria or methodology you applied in selecting the documents that you would reference in your report.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how helpful this will be, but I will try to describe the process by which my reading of documents, over a year ago, results in a report for this Chamber now. I read the documents in the order in which they were presented to me, and sometimes this was quite a straightforward matter, because sometimes they were in paper form and in folders and there was a clear theme as to what they were about. And I can give an example of that: I had a folder of documents at a very early stage in the development of my report which was the -- the title of which way something like "General Cermak and the Press," or "General Cermak's Interviews," that -- that was the -- that was the substance of the thing. So I would go through that folder and I would make notes of anything that I thought was relevant. And what I thought was relevant 15 months ago, I may not have thought was relevant three months ago. Because during the course of reading all these documents, I refined and honed down what I thought I could usefully contribute, so that when I was first reading the documents, the way I was envisaging giving evidence would be to produce a -- a massive document which produced commentary on virtually everything I had seen. But during the course of my research, I decided that there were certain issues that I ought to concentrate on, because they were issues where, in fact, I had expertise, and that's what I had been recruited to deal with. And then later on, as I -- as I said in my methodology, I decided well, actually, probably the best way to deal with this is to take the two issues which are civilian policing, which is my expertise, and the indictment, and see where they were linked, in relation to General Cermak. And that's why the report takes the form it takes now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just to follow up on that, that process of -- of turning the report from a massive document, as you said, commenting on everything, to a document focussed on what you considered to be the issues in the indictment relative --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't actually a report at the early stages. It was -- it was a desk full of pieces of paper with different sections.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And that -- the process of turning it from one to the other, is that a process that you developed on your own or did you have any input from the Cermak Defence on -- with respect to that process?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only time there was an input from the Cermak Defence was after I submitted a draft report, and I got a very short bit of feedback which was, This is too long. So I revisited it. And, in fact, I had to accept that there were areas of my report where I was able to combine different elements in one place and avoid repetition. So actually the final report is slightly shorter than it would have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Was there any other input from the Cermak Defence on that draft report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And just to go back to the document selection process that we had been talking about. Were there any documents that you reviewed that you considered to be relevant to the issues in your report that you did not specifically reference?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were documents that might have what I considered to be some relevance to my report, which were referenced at the draft stage, which have dropped out, certainly. But, by and large, the documents -- well, no, the documents which you see referenced in the report are the documents which I think specifically give an indication to the Chamber of the issues which I'm addressing.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So if I understand your answer - and correct me if I'm wrong - there may be some relevant documents that not referenced in the final report, but those that you considered to be specifically relevant to the issues are included in the report. Is that a fair understanding?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm satisfied with -- that the report, as it stands, references the documents which go to the issues which I discuss. But, of course, I fully anticipate that you may wish to put other documents to me, and I will address those questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At this stage, I'm just trying to understand your process.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept the point. Yes, I understand. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And to go back to the witness transcripts - and if at any point you need to go into private session to answer the question, please indicate that to the Court. I take that, from your earlier answer, that you specifically requested the transcripts of the witnesses who you -- whose evidence you refer to in your report. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I -- I already had witness statements in relation to those particular witnesses, but I asked for the transcripts of their oral testimony so that I could compare and see whether there were any changes in the position. And, of course, from my experience of the other jurisdictions in which I have worked, and will be guided by the Chamber if that is also true here, the oral evidence of witnesses which is subject to challenge under cross-examination generally has greater probative value than the witness statements which are made earlier. But that my not be the case here. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But that was your assumption, that the oral --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my assumption. That the oral --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- that the transcripts had more weight than the statements that you were provided?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the way that I looked at it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And were you provided -- I understand that you were provided with Mr. Theunens' report --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- and that you saw his --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- evidence. Were there any other witness statements or witness evidence that were provided to you through -- in relation to any other witnesses in this case?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, there were a lot of witness statements which I saw in the early days. I had a -- a disc provided to me which contained witness statements from a number of witnesses which were some of the first things that I read. Those witnesses -- I can't give the names, but can I group them to say that they tended to be individual citizens who had been president -- present in the Krajina area at the time of some of the incidents that we're talking about; and internationals, for example, people from the ECMM and UNCIVPOL and that sort of thing, a great lot of witness statements that I read in the earlier stages, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, again, I take it you don't know the basis upon which that witness -- that witness selection was made by the Cermak Defence, in terms of the specific criteria?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, the short answer to your question is, No, I don't. And I know assumptions are not very helpful in judicial proceedings. But my assumption, for what it's worth, was that I was being shown the lot. And certainly a lot of the material I read would not be considered to be directly relevant to General Cermak in his relation with civilian police, but they might, of course, be germane to wider issues that are before the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And what was the basis for your selection of the witnesses that you cited in your report? And, again, if you need to go into private session, please indicate that.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I need to go into private session to answer the question, that the witnesses that I cite give direct evidence about procedures on which I have some knowledge and which I thought were specifically relevant to the issues which I'm addressing in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And with respect to the witness evidence that you have cited in your report, I assume that you have accepted that evidence to be accurate and that's why you have referenced it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily. What I'm trying to do is to make a judgement on the documents which are available to me. I think it is not for me to make an assessment of the quality of the evidence of some of the people to whom you and I are referring slightly elliptically, and, in my submission, it's for the Chamber to make a judgement about the quality of their evidence. My job, as I saw it, was to draw the attention of the Chamber to what I saw as the disparity between certain aspects of the Prosecution case, as outlined in the indictment, and the testimony which was before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So if you didn't make any assessment as to the quality of the evidence, you didn't, for example, look at discrepancies within witnesses' evidence where one piece of evidence of a witness might conflict with something else the witness said. That wasn't part of your process of analysis in terms of what evidence of the witnesses you relied on. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I would be careful -- I wouldn't use the word "analysis" in relation to the process which I applied, simply because in the English speaking police world, at the moment, analysts are individuals who have specific qualifications, and I'm not one of them. They are people who do a two-year course in particular techniques, so I hesitate to use that. But in the ordinary use of the language, I certainly did read statements and compare the statements with the testimony given in court. And whilst I tell this Chamber that I'm not attempting to tell the Chamber what value to place on individual testimony, because the Chamber has seen the witnesses and made its own judgement about them, I didn't see those witnesses, I didn't watch them give evidence. But I do say, and I think I suggest in my report that, that in those areas where I place value on the testimony of the witnesses, it's because what they have said is entirely consistent with my reading, not only of the documents which show the legal and procedural provisions which were extent in the Republic of Croatia at this time, in relation to policing matters, but they're also consistent with my experience as a police officer of the way in which police officers handle direction or attempted direction or liaison and cooperation and issues like that, in relation to other agencies and outside bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, also in your report, at paragraph 1.6, you reference a number of meetings you had with the Cermak Defence which you stated were: "...in order to collect additional material and discuss the progress in the case." Now -- and the footnotes indicate approximately 21 days that you were in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in terms of discussing the progress in the case, I'd like to know more specifically what you spoke about and, in particular, if you discussed anything relating to any of the issues you cover in your report.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, really the reference to progress in the case was to whether particular witnesses had given their evidence. If so, were the transcripts available to me and that sort of thing. I hadn't counted the number of days, but I certainly accept that I spent something in the order of five to six working weeks in The Hague prior to this hearing. Most of that was actually spent sitting at a desk with my laptop and with piles of paper. One of the reasons for that is that can you get far more work done in an office than you can do at home, in a working day. There are no distractions in the office that there are when you're at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And did you have any discussions about the substance of any witnesses or the substance of any documents or the substance of any issues you cover in your report during those discussions?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I was left very much alone as far as that was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you were provided with Mr. Theunens' report and you came and watched his evidence.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: What was the purpose, as far as you are aware, of having you familiarize yourself with Mr. Theunens's evidence and report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have -- maybe it is obvious, but have I never given expert evidence in this Chamber before. And so I think the Defence team -- well, I know the Defence team thought that it was important that I should see what is involved in giving expert evidence. And having watched the cross-examination of Mr. Theunens, I think it was a useful exercise.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss his report or his evidence, in terms of substance, with the Cermak Defence?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And have you ever communicated with General Cermak directly?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm -- I have never spoken to Mr. Cermak. I have seen him through a glass screen, and in the last days, of course, I have seen him across the court. But I have never spoken to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And it's also clear from your report that you had a meeting with the military expert, Mr. Deverell?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: How many meetings did you have with him? Is it just one or a number?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would probably not be right to describe having a meeting with him. We worked in the same office together for a few days last year, and I met him again the day before yesterday. We had dinner together.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And did you and he ever discuss the substance of your report or the substance of the issues you were addressing in your reports?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early days, we discussed what was a military matter and what was a police matter, and we, after some discussion, we agreed that the military police was a military matter and not a police matter. And we discussed the difficulties of reading documents on screens and this sort of thing. And just for the information of the Chamber, having said that I wasn't allowed to see the General's report, I probably ought to add that when we had dinner together, we didn't discuss the case either.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in terms of the military police, that was one part of your draft report, a section of your draft report on the military police you subsequently removed, and I'm wondering what caused you to take that section of your report out.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, having considered, in an early stage, that the military police would be a matter that would be handled by the military expert, I had, nevertheless, read a lot of documents on the military police, because I saw a lot of impact, significantly more tangential impact between the military police issues and the civilian police issues. And also, when I came to collect my ideas together in terms of the indictment, there were areas of the indictment where the terms "military police" and "civilian police" were used together. And I felt an obligation to address the military police issues as part of addressing the issue in that section of the indictment. Then subsequently I thought, Well, actually, I don't have to do that because I can address just the words which are relevant to my expertise. So having been told my report was too long, that was an obvious area to dispense with.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And do you have any idea whether the conclusions you reached with respect to the military police were either consistent or inconsistent with Mr. Deverell's conclusions?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, now I'd like to move to your report itself and the first part of your report which deals with the extent of a garrison commander's authority. And my understanding from your report and -- and from your testimony yesterday, that your -- you looked at whether there was any source for General Cermak's authority over the civilian police in the relevant military documents, such as the service regulations. And you also looked at Ministry of Interior documents. And your conclusion is neither of those two sets of documents provide for any authority of the garrison commander or General Cermak over the civilian police. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I tried to approach the issue from the two sides, and that was the conclusion I reached, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you don't address any other potential sources of General Cermak's authority over the civilian police. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that is fair, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So your view is that General Cermak's authority stemmed only from his position as garrison commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. The documents which I read showed that General Cermak was appointed to his command by the president, that the command was that of the garrison commander, and that's why I looked at documents which might indicate what the authority of the garrison commander was in military terms; and looking specifically, of course, for any impact or any locus which there might be, in relation to civilian policing.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So to put those two together, would it be fair to say that the -- more or less the starting point for your report is that General Cermak's authority stemmed only from his position as garrison commander and that there is no authority of a garrison commander over the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's certainly the conclusion which I reached after examining documents and in relation to what I -- the material that I looked at in the first section of my report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in that first section where you discuss the duties of garrison commanders, according to the rules and regulations, those duties do not include normalisation of life within the garrison, liaising with the press, or liaising with -- liaising between international organisations and the organs of the Croatian government. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I need to revisit the documents to look at the -- all those matters. I was looking specifically, for the purposes of this report, at issues in relation to civilian policing. I don't say that garrison commanders don't have a function in relation to normalisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, if -- if you need to look at any particular document, that's fine. But I -- do you --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying in summary is I'm not challenging your suggestion that General Cermak might have had authority in relation to normalisation issues. I'm not challenging that. I'm just saying that isn't an area in which I would have expertise and address in this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I just -- I'd just like to understand what your -- your understanding -- what your meaning of your report is, and -- and the basis upon which you drew certain conclusions and -- so let me put the question this way. Do you recall seeing any duty of a garrison commander that related to normalisation of life, liaising with the press, or liaising between international organisations and the organs of the Croatian government in any of the relevant HV or Ministry of Defence documents you reviewed - and please, if you need to refer to any documents --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, like I said, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, throughout your report, you have mentioned some of these duties in passing, and I'd just like to mention a few of them to you. You stated that General Cermak played a coordinating and representative point of contact role in relation to post-conflict normalisation. That's at paragraph 2.3. At paragraph 3.81 you stated that General Cermak's role in relation to these matters can best be seen as a public face, be it for the press or for the international interlocutors. At paragraph 3.88, you stated: "It should, in my opinion, be interpreted in the light of General Cermak's acknowledged role in relation to the international community and UNCRO in particular." At paragraph 3.94 you referred to the latter's, referring to General Cermak's international liaison role. In paragraph 3.6 the you stated: "In my opinion, this is because the nature of General Cermak's coordinating role was either between the internationals and the Croats or related to domestic functions pertaining to normalisation." And from my reading of your report, nowhere in your report do you specifically explain how you reached these conclusions that General Cermak had these types of roles. Is that -- is that fair?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is entirely fair. I have seen no document which provides some sort of legal authority or provenance or direction which gives General Cermak the sort of authority in the issues which you have just referred to. My assessment of his role in relation to that comes not from any cited document which gives General Cermak authority in those specific areas; it comes from my reading of the documents as to what he actually did and the authority which appears to have been accorded to him by those with whom he was dealing. In other words, the actions of the people involved in playing out this -- the scenes which are familiar to the Chamber appear to accord that sort of authority and responsibility and role to General Cermak. But, of course, you're quite right to say that I do not, in my report, indicate any written authority for him to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, are you able to identify, now, which specific evidentiary sources you relied on to reach your implicit conclusions in your report, that General Cermak had these roles?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot quote court numbers, but I can guide the Chamber towards the sort of documents. In relation to the international point of contact, there are, in my submission, numerous documents which indicate that, for example, Brigadier Forand of Canada took the view very early on that General Cermak was the man to whom he should go to get things done. And there is correspondence visible to the Chamber, which I didn't cite but which I read, numerous examples. For example, General Cermak seeks the assistance of Brigadier Forand to remove abandoned and broken down vehicles from the road. He seeks the assistance of General Forand with dealing with either waterworks or sewage or something of that sort. Brigadier Forand is -- uses General Cermak as a point of contact for dealing with his issues and, of course, the notorious one which has been before the Chamber before and doubtless will resurface later on is the theft of the UN vehicles, where before Brigadier Forand realises that General Cermak can't actually achieve some of the things which he hopes and goes to General Gotovina, Forand uses General Cermak as his avenue. Take another example. We discussed yesterday communication from the ICRC who are looking for information about some crime matters. Now, I have told the Chamber that, in my professional opinion, General Cermak wasn't the man who dealt with crime. But that's not to say that he wasn't the man who could communicate information being it to the international community. So these are the sorts of incidents which make me take that view in relation to international liaison. So far as the press is concerned, quite early on in my research, I had a folder of documents which are transcripts of General Cermak's interviews with -- I hesitate to try and pronounce "Slobodna Dalmacija" and various other newspapers. There are also videos, which I think are exhibits within the Chamber, of General Cermak giving television interviews. Now, as I said before, I can't tell this Chamber, Here's a document which says the garrison commander is in charge of giving television interviews. I don't think it exists. I would be prepared to be corrected on that, but I haven't seen it if it does. But I have seen the evidence of what General Cermak did, and that is the basis upon which I make the remarks in my report about those functions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, could I seek clarification of one of the earlier answers. I'll read a portion of your answer, Mr. Albiston. You said: "My assessment of his role in relation to that," and you were referring to the other issues, "comes not from any cited document which gives General Cermak authority in those specific areas; it comes from my reading of the documents as to what he actually did and the authority which appears to have been accorded to him by those with whom he was dealing." And then you continued: "In other words, the actions of the people involved in playing out this -- the scenes which are familiar to the Chamber appear to accord that sort of authority and responsibility and role to General Cermak." Now, in the first part of what I read, you say, The way in which he acted, and the way in which he was apparently perceived by others, who would then also accorded him authority, when you said "In other words," it seems that the emphasis shifts from according authority by observers though who perceived his activity rather than his own activity. Is that what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Mr. President, that I entirely understand the distinction. I think what I -- what my -- I'm saying to the Court is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but let me then try ... You gave one of the examples, an interview. Now, if the journalist addressed General Cermak and say, Could you give us an interview, that could be perceived as how journalists looked at the authority and the function of Mr. Cermak. If I say, There will be a press conference this afternoon, then we have an active role played by the actor, Mr. Cermak - it's just an example, not to say that that this is the way how interviews were organised. But, you see, there are two different aspects: The one is by your own actions to create the impression of authority; and the other one is that observers, without any clear action triggering this perception, perceive you as the man in charge. Now, in your answer, in the first part of your answer, you specifically referred to what he actually did; whereas, when you then summarised it or rephrase it "in other words," did you intend to leave that part out, or is it still fully present? So is there any shift from his activity triggering the impression of authority to others, without any activity that would trigger that impression, more or less according authority to him, I would say spontaneously more or less?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, I'm grateful for that. And I understand what the distinction was that Mr. President was highlighting. I'm afraid my answer to counsel wasn't quite as sophisticated as that. And basically what I was saying was both. And I wasn't attempting to describe a chronological process by which one side of that equation took place before the other side. I suppose the obvious thing is, if a general gives a press interview, and I'm a press man and I turn up the next day, I think, Well, there's a general who talks to the press, I'll go and talk to him. So the process can be sort of mutually supporting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, it's clear now from your answers, Mr. Albiston, that you more or less inferred that General Cermak had authority over certain tasks, based on the evidence that he was actually carrying out those tasks in fact. Is that -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I would say it's quite fair to say that a certain number of the tasks and the sort of things that you have spoken about were matters in which - and I choose my words more carefully now after Mr. President's intervention - but either which Mr. Cermak or General Cermak saw as his responsibility and was willing to accept as his responsibility, or which others chose to heap upon him as his responsibility because he was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you covered the first two roles that I mentioned, in terms of evidentiary sources, which were international point of contact and liaising with the press. What evidentiary sources did you rely on to draw the implicit conclusion that General Cermak had a role to normalise life within the garrison?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would need to refer to the document which I think is round about D34, because I think there 's a paragraph, or two paragraphs, in there which talk about the garrison commander's role in garrison life, which I think could be used by the Chamber as -- as a source of authority for General Cermak's role in relation to normalisation. But I don't say that that is specific to this issue, and it wasn't one which I was addressing specifically in my report. I would base the comments in my report more on the documents which demonstrate that General Cermak played a role in normalisation. By "normalisation" what I'm referring to are things like re-establishing water, electricity, the re-opening of what are rather quaintly referred to as the "cake shops" and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In terms of evidentiary sources, are you able to point to any?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would need to ask the indulgence of the Chamber to highlight or identify the particular documents. But if there's a dispute as to whether there are documents before the Chamber which show General Cermak playing a role in relation to, for example, issues of accommodation, power, clearing up of animal carcasses, and dealing with dead bodies, if those are -- if it's an issue whether General Cermak had any role in that through the documents, then I would have to go and look for the documents. But I didn't think that was an issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Really, just to be clear, it's a conclusion that you draw in your report and it's implicit; it's not something that you directly address.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So I'm really aimed at making transparent what is not transparent on your report --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- as opposed to exploring those issues in substance.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that. And if counsel thinks it's a defect in the report that those assumptions are not supported by documents, then I apologise. But the reason, of course, is that I did not think that that was an issue which was in dispute between the Prosecution and the Defence. And it wasn't an area which I thought was particularly relevant to my comments on General Cermak in relation to civilian policing. That's why there's no citation of documents to support those statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And nowhere in your report do you mention or discuss any discrepancy between these types of tasks that you have ascribed to General Cermak in your report and the tasks that you cite as those of a -- formal tasks of a garrison commander. And I'm wondering if it ever crossed your mind, as you were preparing your report, that there was such a discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, it didn't. I didn't see this as issue which was one for me to deal with directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, if -- I need some seven or eight minutes for some procedural matters soon. We are close to 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is as good a time as any. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is as good a time as ... Then we will not bother or bother you with the matters we have on our agenda, Mr. Albiston. Could you please already follow the Usher so that we can deal with some procedural matters. We'd like to see you back in approximately half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first matter is about scheduling for next week. The Chamber has looked in its agenda, and possibilities for sitting whole days next week would be Monday morning and afternoon, with the following observation: That, for the last hour of Monday, not all three Judges would be available. So for the last portion, most likely the last session of Monday, we'd have to consider to sit under Rule 15 bis. We have an opportunity to sit Tuesday, the whole of the day. But if we would start at 9.00 in the morning, the first two hours, that is the first session, it's only possible to sit under Rule 15 bis. Then, I understand, on Wednesday, we could continue until and including the first afternoon session. Adding this up altogether would mean that if we would not use Rule 15 bis, that, on Monday, we'd have five sessions without 15 bis; six sessions with 15 bis; and we still have to see whether this could be full sessions or not, because usually if we're sitting a whole day, the schedule is adapted slightly. For Thursday -- Tuesday, the 10th, it would mean, when using 15 bis, six sessions; without 15 bis, five sessions. For Wednesday, it would mean four sessions as a maximum, in view of the request made by the Prosecution. To sit under Rule 15 bis requires that the remaining Judges, which would not be the same during these two days, that the other Judges would decide that it would be in the interests of justice to continue hearing the case. I make the following observation: That for expert witnesses, it might be a little bit less sensitive to read the testimony or to look at the tapes of the testimony compared to witnesses of fact. But the Judges would have to decide. The parties are invited to see whether they can work out a schedule such that, with or without relying on 15 bis, they think they could present the evidence in-chief and in cross to the Chamber within these time-frames. Because, if, finally, we'd need Thursday and Friday anyhow, then the Chamber is not very much inclined to do the gymnastic exercise and the whole of the rescheduling the first three days. So, therefore, the Chamber is willing to consider it and will seriously consider if that would be needed to sit - and when I'm talking about the Chamber, of course, it is it always the two Judges remaining - we'll seriously consider to hear the case under Rule 15 bis if there is a firm commitment by the parties that, by then, we would conclude the evidence of next week's witness on Wednesday, the 11th, after the first afternoon session. This is not a ruling, but this is an invitation. If there's such a firm commitment, we'll then further consider -- we will then know whether you would need the 15 bis sessions or whether you could even do without. If you would need them, the Judges will then consider whether Rule 15 bis would be applied or not. That, as far as scheduling is concerned. I have to deliver two decisions. The first one is the Chamber's decision on protective measures for Witness AG-10. On the 25th of September, 2009, the Gotovina Defence requested the protective measures of pseudonym and under-seal treatment for Witness AG-10. The Gotovina Defence argued that Witness AG-10 was concerned about testifying publicly and did not want his identity as a witness divulged to the public. On the 9th of October, 2009, the Prosecution responded to the request, not objecting to it. Neither the Cermak Defence nor the Markac Defence responded to the request. Witness AG-10's statement was admitted, pursuant to Rule 92 bis of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, on the 16th of September, 2009. As the Chamber has held in previous decisions on protective measures, the party seeking protective measures for a witness must demonstrate an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness or the witness's family, should it become known that the witness has given evidence before the Tribunal. The question of whether to grant protective measures involves a delicate balance between the right of the accused to a public trial, on the one hand; and the interests and need for protection and privacy for victims and witnesses on the other. In this respect, the Chamber is mindful that the granting of protective measures does not negatively affect an accused's other fair trial rights, such as the right to examine witnesses against him. Even though the granting of protective measures is, and should be, the exception to the rule of a public trial, the threshold for when it should be granted cannot be set too high. The Chamber must, therefore, make a risk assessment, and inherent in such an assessment, is applying a certain level of caution and erring on the safe side. Witness AG-10 expressed fear for the safety of his family and himself, all of whom live in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The witness's testimony provides information about Serbia's involvement in, amongst others, the Krajina and about the distribution of weapons to local Serbs, including within Croatia, and the use of propaganda against Croatia. The witness feels threatened by persons who fled from Croatia after Operation Storm and who are currently residing in Bosnia and Herzegovina, particularly in the area where his family lives. The Chamber considers that the witness's testimony might antagonise persons who reside in that area. The witness also provides compromising and even incriminating evidence about several named individuals in positions of influence. Witness AG-10, based on negative reactions of concern persons in the past, is convinced that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina cannot provide him with the necessary protection. For the foregoing reasons, and bearing in mind the general considerations mentioned earlier, and the fact that none of the parties opposed the request, the Chamber finds that the Gotovina Defence demonstrated an objectively grounded risk to the security of Witness AG-10, should it become known that the witness has given evidence before this Tribunal. The Chamber therefore grants the motion for protective measures for Witness AG-10 and instructs the Registrar to keep Witness AG-10's statement under seal. And this concludes the Chamber's decision to grant protective measures for Witness AG-10.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, before the break, you had stated that you did not consider that this discrepancy between the tasks and authorities General Cermak had, and the normal tasks of a garrison commander, you stated that you did not consider that it was an "... issue which was one for me to deal with directly." And it's right that nowhere in your report do you consider what were the sources of General Cermak's authority to carry out these tasks that aren't covered by the tasks of a garrison commander. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a fair comment. The documents which I studied which describe the functions of the garrison commander are perhaps best commented on by a military expert. But my reading of them, in terms of the ordinary language used, led me to believe that they were drafted with a situation in mind which was a peacetime garrison, and that some of the conditions which were extent at the time when General Cermak was the garrison commander were not entirely what was anticipated by the people who drafted those regulations. But I think -- I hesitate to go there because I don't think that is an area of my expertise.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And do you mention, in passing in your report, that a garrison commander under the rules is designated by the Main Staff. But you mention as well that General Cermak was appointed by President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But it appears from your report that you didn't consider this to be of any relevance or at -- or that it was outside the scope of your expertise, this -- the fact that General Cermak was appointed directly by the president, as opposed to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- from memory, I think I mentioned his appointment by the president in the report, but you're certainly right to say that I don't analyse or draw attention or comment on that particular aspect, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, if, in the course of President Tudjman assigning General Cermak to be garrison commander, if he had personally assigned to General Cermak tasks and responsibilities beyond that of a normal garrison commander, that information would be relevant - would it not? - to determining the scope of General Cermak's authority and the nature of his assignment. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly in relation to military aspects, yes. In relation to civilian police aspects, I think there are reasons which come out in my report as to why I did not examine any additional authorities, because the authorities, in relation to civilian policing and the criminal justice system, seem, to me, to be quite clear from the documents which I studied. But if -- if you are suggesting to me that there were authorities implicit in some arrangement between the president and General Cermak of which I am unaware, then I accept that may be the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just to follow up on that answer, you seem to suggest that President Tudjman couldn't have granted General Cermak, personally, some authority over the civilian police. And I'd like to know if my understanding of your answer is correct, and if so, what's the basis for your conclusion that President Tudjman couldn't have done this, either in law or in fact.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't -- I don't say anything. I don't try to circumscribe the powers of the president of the Republic of Croatia as they existed in 1995 and impose limitations on the president. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just to be clear, you're not a position to do that --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- based on your expertise. Thank you. Now, the Chamber has received evidence that President Tudjman did assign General Cermak tasks that go beyond that of a garrison commander. And my question for you is whether you saw any evidence of that assignment.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any evidence before the Chamber or otherwise, which provides documentary authority for General Cermak to undertake those additional tasks, which he did undertake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, if we are talking about seeing any evidence, that may create some confusion. We have documentary evidence - and I understood from your answer, Mr. Albiston, that you didn't see evidence before the Chamber or otherwise which provides documentary authority, therefore, you apparently "seeing evidence" is understood by you as seeing documents which would support.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whereas, seeing evidence could also mean reading transcripts of oral testimony. And I urge both you and Ms. Gustafson to be as precise as possible so that we do not have any -- any problems in how -- what it exactly means to see evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I accept the distinction, Mr. President, and perhaps the best short answer would have been, No. But I was trying to assist the Chamber by confirming for Ms. Gustafson that I am not aware of any statutory or procedural or authoritative document enshrined in the laws and procedures of the Republic of Croatia of the of the type which Ms. Gustafson was alluding to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you -- are you aware of any evidence which is not, by nature, statutory or documentary --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. JUDGE ORIE -- which would support the proposition by Ms. Gustafson that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- special authority could have been given by the president to Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Again, the short answer is, No, I'm not. If Ms. Gustafson wishes to draw my attention to any matters, it may that be that I would recognise them. But as I sit here, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, again, just to pick up on your last answer where you stated that you were not aware of any statutory or procedural or authoritative document of the type that I was alluding to - and I actually didn't allude to any particular kind of document - and it brings me to the question, Do you have any reason to doubt that President Tudjman could have assigned General Cermak authorities, significant authorities, in an informal way, rather than a statutory or legal, procedural way?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I'm not going to go into this in detail because it's clear from your answers this isn't an area that you have addressed or -- and this material that I'm alluding to isn't something that you have specifically reviewed. But I would like to point to one example, which is a transcript of a meeting between General Cermak and President Tudjman in 1999 at which they discussed General Cermak's assignment in Knin and they include, in the scope of this assignment, cooperation with the international community, infrastructure, return, life, hospitals, keeping order, preventing disorder, and mine clearance.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And for the record, I'm referring to P1144.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I take it from your earlier answers you didn't see that particular document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's certainly not one that's cited in my report. But if could I see the document, it -- it might be one that I saw at an early stage of my review of document, yes. I'm certainly not telling the Chamber that I've never seen this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Perhaps it would make sense, then, just to pull up P1144.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing any transcripts of meetings that President Tudjman held? There are a number of them in this case, and I'm wondering if that was a body of material that you recall seeing.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen a document, and possibly more than one document, of the type which you are describing. Whether this particular one is one that I have seen or not, I don't know. I'm -- if I see the text, it may or may not refresh my memory. But I'm certainly aware that such documents exist, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, the cover page is there now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could move to page 4 in the English and page 6 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you can see the discussion takes place near the -- in the top third of the page. Do you recall seeing that before?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that whilst I cannot say, Yes, I definitely saw this document, reading the text of the first half of the page, it does look familiar to me. The ideas that -- the general context does look familiar to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
