utterances.text: Now, if -- if General Cermak's tasks assigned directly from President Tudjman included keeping order and preventing disorder, that would be relevant information to determining the scope of General Cermak's authority and the scope of his authority over the civilian police. Wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly if the provisions of the prevailing law enable the president to make those determinations, it would be relevant, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, again, you're not really in a position to say whether President Tudjman couldn't have affected that in an informal way?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't -- well, sorry, I was anticipating a wrong question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I beg your pardon. I was anticipating that the question would end in a slightly different way, and that's why I started answering, and I shouldn't do that. I don't know about the informal relationships between the president and General Cermak at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you - I just want to be clear on this - you can't opine on President Tudjman's formal or informal authority over the structures of government?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the formal side, I haven't seen any document which suggests that he could accord to General Cermak the sort of authority which you're suggesting. I'm not saying he couldn't; I'm saying I haven't seen any documents to prove that he could. On the informal side, I think that's probably a political judgement. I'm not qualified to say. And I -- you know, I don't know from the documents whether he could or he couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Would you agree from the documents that President Tudjman did have a fair amount of authority over the government and the government ministers, including the interior minister?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And just to conclude this -- this part of my questions, you don't consider anywhere in your report whether General Cermak may have held some authority over the civilian police by virtue of his assignment of tasks directly by President Tudjman. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't address that proposition, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, if we could bring up D589.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is the document, the one document you cite in the first part of your report on the garrison commander's authority that is not one of the relevant laws or regulations. And that's at paragraph 3.13 of your report. And in your report, you state that this document supports the conclusion that General Cermak was not in a position of command or control in relation to the civilian police. And yesterday you stated, in relation to this document, at page 23.782: "... to me the significance of that is that if General Cermak, as garrison commander, featured in any way in the Ministry of the Interior or civilian policing hierarchy, surely there would be no need to ask for civilian police officers to be present in meetings which he chaired." Now, this document, as you know, is dated the 28th of August, 1995, and I presume you are aware that, at this point in time, the civilian police were attending regular, virtually daily meetings with General Cermak in his office, his regular meetings. Right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware that they did attend meetings, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we have the text -- I think I'm on the wrong page here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think it should be --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the meetings that this document refers to are just the meetings that General Cermak are holding with members of international organisations. It's not referring to meetings generally. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the -- that's what I take from the words on the document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And on its face, this document doesn't say anything about whether General Cermak can command the civilian police, right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't -- it doesn't state categorically whether he can or he can't. What I suggested in evidence was that the inference to be drawn from this is that he wasn't in a particular chain of command; namely, the Ministry of Interior chain of command, which the civilian police were in.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's the conclusion that I'd like to understand a bit better, because I don't understand what exactly is it that shows that he's not in a particular chain of command. You don't mean that the civilian police would have to be present at every meeting General Cermak holds, for him to be in a position of command over them, do you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I'm not saying that. What I'm say is, If you're asking at a higher level to get people into somebody else's meetings, if that somebody else happened to be in the same chain of command as you, why -- why would you ask?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So, because Mr. Tomurad, the author of this report, wasn't able to directly interfere and have assign civilian police officers to attend meetings with General Cermak --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that's the inference you're trying to draw --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- that's -- that's the basis?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, just in terms of the substance of this document --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think if we move to the next page, or the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Where it says that: "The purpose for this request is to ensure that the police are informed about all agreements and" --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: "... conclusions reached which will enable them to organise, plan tasks and duties from their purview accordingly." Now, one interpretation of this document is that General Cermak is able to enter into agreements directly with members of international organisations that the members of the MUP will then have to implement on the ground. Is that a reasonable interpretation of this document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I think you could -- you could probably go further than that and say that a concern which Mr. Tomurad appears to be expressing is that information regarding the concerns of members of different organisations who might be loosely termed the "international community" were coming into the police second-hand, and it might be better for the purposes of police organising their patrols patterns, for example, if they heard some of the international's concerns directly. That's -- I mean, that's one inference that I think you can draw from this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I actually wasn't asking about concerns of internationals. I was referring to the words of the document which states: "... agreements and conclusions reached ..." And I infer from that that General Cermak is entering into agreements and -- that will affect directly the work of the MUP in their absence, and this is why Mr. Tomurad is making that request.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, you could interpret it that Mr. Tomurad wants the police to make their own decisions or, as it says, "... plan tasks and duties from their purview accordingly," yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go now to P38, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The document that is about to come up is a weekly report by Mr. Al-Alfi. And -- for the 2nd to 8th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 3 of the English and page 2 in the B/C/S, please. And about -- Is this page 3 of the English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says 4 of 6 on what I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: There we go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you can see about a little past halfway down the page he is describing a meeting with General Cermak and it says: "During the meeting, we raised with General Cermak the question of continuing looting and burning of houses in the area. We further raised specific cases of recent murders which were brought to his attention and asked for the results of the investigation by the Croatian authorities. General Cermak did not deny the continuation of such activities, and said that strict orders have been issued to arrest those who commit such crimes."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we go to the last sentence of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: "General Cermak agreed to give his instructions for more joint patrolling between UNCIVPOL and the Croatian police, particularly in the remote villages." Now, this document is consistent with the previous document in suggesting that General Cermak has the authority to commit the civilian police to take certain operational actions at his meetings he holds with internationals. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, forgive me, I have to disagree with that interpretation of document. My reading of this document is that it indicates that General Cermak gave the impression that he had that authority. And I think it's fully understandable in the circumstances. If, as I say in my report, as a result of my examination of documents, General Cermak did not have the sort of authority which he appears to be crediting himself with in this document, and that's my position, it is, nevertheless, not at all surprising that he should say something slightly different or be understood to be saying something slightly different in these circumstances. If he is performing an international liaison role and matters are being drawn to his attention, the natural result of which ought to be increased or more effective patrolling or check-points by the civilian police, then, irrespective of whether General Cermak had any genuine established authority over the civilian police, I would expect him to say, Yes I will get something done about this. I wouldn't expect him to say, Well, I'll ask the police what they think and whether they can do it, or anything like that. I mean, that's not the way people behave in these circumstances in my experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you think these statements by General Cermak are deliberate misrepresentations of his authority?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think deliberate misrepresentation is a fair way. I think that's an unnecessarily pejorative emphasis, but I think it's certainly not the case on the basis on the documents that I have seen that General Cermak was referring to any genuine authority he had to do this. But it's quite normal. I would expect him to go back from a meeting like this and to say to representatives of the civilian police, Look, there is what's happening. This is what these people are saying. What can you do about it? And the police, then, under the authorities which I describe in my report, would take the necessary action. And indeed there are documents which we talked about yesterday which emanate through the Ministry of the Interior chain of command and the Ministry of Defence chain of command insofar as it refers to the military police and the efforts of men under the command of Major-General Mate Lausic, which show these responses. And there are meetings which take place at all levels between the civilian police and the military police to deal with precisely these issues. And the military police chain of commands and the civilian police chain of commands discuss performance at check-point, discuss whether people are turning up for patrols --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Albiston. Sorry. Just to get back to your initial answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I said: "Do you think these statements by General Cermak are deliberate misrepresentations of his authority?" And your answer was: "I don't think deliberate misrepresentation is a fair way." I think you said to put it --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now -- and then you went on to discuss possible -- I believe, possible motivations for making that statement.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I'd just like you to put the motivations aside for a moment an answer directly the question whether you think these statements by General Cermak, such as, that he will give his instructions for more joint patrolling between civilian police and UNCIVPOL, are deliberate misrepresentations of his authority.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that they are an overinflated representation of his actual position. But, in terms of the results that might be achieved, namely, that if he passed the information to the relevant channels, something might be done about it, it is it not a misrepresentation in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, I am addressing you and the witness as well. I have heard now de jure de facto authority. I have heard the term "genuine authority." In the last answer, "overinflated representation of his actual position." Could we, under all circumstances, try to clearly distinguish between what kind of authority we are talking about. Because I get the feeling that you are more focussed on de facto authority exercised, whether or not supported by any legal instrument, instruction, et cetera; whereas, I get the feeling that Mr. Albiston is often, in his answer, very much focussing on what he calls genuine authority, which I understand de jure authority. Let's try to get these matters as clear as possible. Because it is a repeating source of -- of -- well, not confusion, perhaps, but at least not 100 per cent understanding. I think for 50 or 60 per cent you're talking about the same matter, but then for the remaining 40 per cent you're talking about different matters. Could you please try to keep this - and I'm also addressing, you, Mr. Albiston - could you try to make this as clear as possible in every question and in every answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I will try to do so. But if I fail to make that explicit, I'm always referring to authority in fact in this context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It takes two to tango, I do understand that, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, again, I would just like to go back to my question and your answer, and you stated when I asked you again whether these were deliberate misrepresentations: "I would say that they are an overinflated representation of his actual position." And, again, I understand your view to be that, in fact, General Cermak could not issue instructions for more joint patrolling between civilian police and UNCIVPOL?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- in view of what the President says, I will try to be as exact as possible in my use of language. But I think there are grey areas when we're talking about misrepresentation. I argued yesterday, and in my report, particularly from a de jure perspective, about General Cermak's authority or absence of it, in relation to the civilian police, and I also touched on the de facto aspects. In relation to this particular phrase, what I would say is this. It -- it does not impact, in my view, on the conclusions which I reached about General Cermak's de jure authority, or absence of it, in relation to the civilian police, what this he did, where they patrolled, where they set up check-points, how they based, and so on. It may indicate that because of his central position and his liaison position and the charisma or authority which goes with the rank of Colonel General, and the fact that he was a source of information in relation to certain matters for the civilian police, be a natural follow-on that what he said would influence the conduct of the police in the discharge of their duties by -- in giving them information which would enable them to determine their patrols patterns or the location of their check-points or the concentration of their resources or that sort of thing. I hope that helps on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, a little, but, actually not really, because what General Cermak is saying in this document is that he will give his instructions for more joint patrolling. And what you're talking about is giving information. And yet you say it's not a deliberate misrepresentation, and I simply can't square these.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it's -- perhaps we're playing with words. I think it is an inflation of his authority. Deliberate misrepresentation implies that General Cermak was in some way trying to deceive other people about what he would do, about what the outcome of the meeting might be. Now, it seems to me that if the outcome of the meeting is that police patrolling patterns will change or that police check-point locations will change because General Cermak gives the civilian police information which enables them to do their job more effectively, that might be the same outcome as if General Cermak, being in the chain of command of the police, went back to the police station and said, Right, this is what you're going to do. The outcome might be the same, and I wouldn't blame General Cermak for using language which attracts kudos to his position as garrison commander and international point of contact. But, deliberate misrepresentation, I think that's a -- yeah, as it judgement. But in my judgement, that's, perhaps, a bit unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we should not spend too much time on whether it's a deliberate misrepresentation or not. Mr. Albiston, you have given a picture of two situations. The one was General Cermak, in the follow-up of this meeting, giving information; and the other option was that General Cermak, as you said, being in the chain of command would give orders or instructions. You used the word, "Right, this is what you're going to do." Now, would you agree with me that there is a third option, that not being in the chain of command, nevertheless, giving instructions, orders, whatever you call it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That can happen. I see no evidence that that did happen, although there are certainly documents which I'm sure counsel is going to bring do my attention at some time, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that you clearly explained why, in your report, why all kind of documents which were phrased as orders should not be understood as orders. So it comes as a bit of a surprise to me that you say it can happen, but I haven't seen it. Because I think you dealt with several of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was trying to answer what I understood to be a hypothetical question by Mr. President; namely, could you have a situation in which somebody doesn't have authority to give an order but does so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I was trying to relate that back to my reading of the documents and what had happened in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, in such a situation. Because what we are talking about is the effect. You explained to us that sometimes providing information - and you give a lot of circumstances which could then have a certain effect. You said it is possible that in the conduct of those, in performing their tasks, would be influenced by that. Now, I do take it that in the other situation, if you are in a chain of command, that the effect would be more or less self-explanatory, because if are you in command, if you give orders, that is supposed to have an impact, an effect on the conduct of your subordinates. Now, would the situation in which an instruction or an order would have been given, even if there may not be a de jure basis for that, would that have or could that have a similar effect as the situation in which you inform the police about certain matters, which you said could, under the very specific circumstances - and you mentioned quite a couple of conditions - could have an effect. Would it be any different if you would have the same rank, if the same situation, the same -- well, all the other conditions. If you would issue instructions or orders, could that have the same effect as providing information to the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think it's fair to say that you could have similar outcomes through two different activities. And to take a hypothetical example, you could inform the police that a murder had taken place in a house, and could you inform police that there was significant disorder every Friday night at a particular place. Or, not having any authority to do so, you could order police to go and investigate a murder at a house, or you could order police to go and patrol in an area where there was significant disorder on Friday night. The outcome of the two activities might actually be the same, but the process by which the decision was taken would be different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, then, the next question would be, you more or less suggested that where, in this report, Mr. Cermak is reported to have said, I will give instructions. You said, Well, he would have given information and you explained what effect that would have. Do you have any -- any information or any reason to choose for whether he actually did give instructions, or whether he did give information, or perhaps nothing at all, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In relation to the document which is on the screen now and about which Ms. Gustafson has been asking me, the answer is, No, I don't. There are other occasions in which General Cermak, according to the documents before the Chamber, makes what might be consider to be or, in my submission, would be considered to be fairly bold pronouncements about what he will and will not do. And I think we looked at a document yesterday which described an incident in which UN observers were stopped at a check-point in circumstances which led General Cermak to announce that this was all wrong and that the police officers involved would be punished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the implication is that, you know, he had authority to do these things. Well, I'm saying that sometimes General Cermak seems to be saying things about which he doesn't have the authority to speak in quite the terms which he is reported as having spoken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But in relation to this document --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In relation to this document, yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... if we are talking about whether he would have given information or instructions or orders or whatever, that has a speculative element in it because you do not have any specific information about the situation --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't -- there may be another document which counsel will produce which will show a follow-up to this, and I may have seen it. But, sitting as I do now, I can't anticipate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm, at this moment, trying to find out what exactly -- what exactly is assumption and what is knowledge and concrete information. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, I'd like to move on now to the next section of your report, which is about the police structures and the MUP. And most of this is about the formal MUP structure and your conclusion that the garrison commander has no role in that structure. And it may be clear to you now by now, but if it's not, just to make it clear, the Prosecution doesn't take issue with any of those conclusions about General Cermak's role in the formal structure. And my questions, as I've indicated, will focus more on the factual situation. Now in paragraph 3.34 of this section, you refer to the extent to which General Cermak is mentioned in MUP documents. And one of the things you said was that notes made by Kotar-Knin Police Administration Deputy Commander Zvonko Gambiroza acknowledge the problems being experienced by General Cermak as a result of the continuous insisting by Brigadier Forand in relation to the missing UNCRO vehicles.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And do you recall, now, whether that is the only reference to General Cermak in Mr. Gambiroza's diary or whether there are others?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So if I suggested to that you there were 15 references to General Cermak in this diary that covers the period between 12 August and 21 September, you don't have any reason to doubt that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, you have indicated that, in a later paragraph of your report which is 3.41, and it's clear from the evidence that the Knin civilian police leadership attended meetings with General Cermak on a daily or virtually daily basis. And my question for you is whether you would agree that that was the primary means of communication and the primary point of contact between General Cermak and the Knin police, based on what you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Significant, certainly. I wouldn't change primary. That wasn't the conclusion I came to.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in light of the fact that there are no minutes or transcripts from those meetings, at least none that we have, would you agree that the bulk of General Cermak's communication or at least a large part of it with the civilian police is not documented?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would accept that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, now, yesterday you were asked what you would have expected to have seen within the MUP documentation, if General Cermak were in command or control of the civilian police, in light of your experience in numerous policing systems, and you said: "Well, I would expect General Cermak's name to appear on a significant array of documents of different types. For example, I would expect to see his name on instructions, policy documents, orders going out to the civilian police. I would expect to see his name on orders transferring or appointing senior police officers. I would expect to see his name on reports going up the Ministry of the Interior chain of command."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, my question is, in terms of your experience in different policing systems and the expectations that you may have as a result, do you have any first-hand experience or knowledge with a situation such as the one that the Prosecution alleges in this case, namely, that a high-ranking military officer is granted authority directly by the head of state and supreme commander, and, as a result, exercises authority, in fact, over the civilian police in a particular area?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, again, on these meetings, daily meetings between General Cermak and the civilian police, among others, you state at paragraph 3.41: "Another key example of General Cermak's relationship of cooperation with the civilian police can be seen in the context of the meetings held at the garrison in Knin. Representatives of the Kotar-Knin police administration," and you corrected that phrase, "attended regular, sometimes daily, meetings chaired by General Cermak." And you state: "In my experience, in policing circles, chairing a multi-agency meeting does not imply the authority to direct the work of all the agencies which are represented at the meeting." Now, it appears that you seem to conclude that the fact of chairing a meeting is key in terms of cooperation, and I'd like do understand that a bit better. You would agree that a person can chair a meeting in circumstances where they have authority over the participants, and they can chair a meeting in circumstances where they don't have authority but can merely cooperate with the participants, right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The chair of a meeting might have direct authority, or the chair of a meeting might have status but not authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So what caused you to draw the conclusion in this paragraph that General Cermak's chairing of these meetings was a key example of his relationship of cooperation with the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was an opportunity for him to have direct conversation about day-to-day issues. And my experience of working in fairly difficult security environments in which the police and the military work closely with each other is that daily meetings between representatives of the agencies is very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, if you -- I take you back to one of your previous answers, if you would not mind. "Yes, the chair of a meeting might have direct authority." Which I understood to be de jure or formal authority. "... or the chair of a meeting might have status but not authority." I understand the last authority, no formal authority but status, would not exclude de facto authority would, it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it wouldn't. It would give weight to what was said. It would give ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, or even people might be inclined to do what you suggest, request, order, instruct, ask them to do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think the -- my experience at these meetings is that where a person has status and a bit of charisma and leadership qualities, then they can excerpt influence on people over whom they don't actually have direct authority. And they can perhaps guide the meeting towards a conclusion which suits them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What -- the reason I took you back to this answer is I earlier invited you to always make clear, when you were talking about authority, what kind of authority you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now you introduced a new status concept, which is not in every respect - I'm not saying entirely the same but not in every respect to be distinguished from de facto authority - and I again ask you to be very clear in the use of those terms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And what I meant by status, status in relation to someone who is chairing a meeting, if I from the army, and I go to a meeting with a policeman, even though I am a soldier and do not form part of the police rank structure, if the person who is chairing the meeting from the policing side is a sergeant, I might accord that person less authority and status in an informal way than if that person were a chief superintendent. That's all I was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What you say is that it depends on the circumstances that even if there is no formal authority that the influence that a person chairing such a meeting tells what should be done and then preferably by the others and not by himself, that that could come close to a situation of de facto authority, whatever the words used, asking, requesting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, certainly a good chair can influence the outcome of a meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And it need not depend on de jure authority, to achieve the objectives in chairing a meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I notice that when de facto authority comes up, that you often use the language of having an influence on the behaviour of others. I'm not going to make it any linguistic debate at this moment. But if you see a clear distinction between the two, you're invited to tell me what exactly is the difference, where you say it may have an influence on -- on what others are doing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- or inclined to do and to what accident that it different from a de facto authority, so that it's clear for me how you use your language. Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honours, just following on from Your Honours observations, in terms of a distinction, clearly the distinction between de jure and de facto, but also the clear distinction between, at least in law, influence and de facto, which I know Your Honour will be aware. But I'm concerned, given the flexibility of the language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that. But often when the word de facto is used, I hear that in response that the witness responds by saying that something has an influence. I am trying to understand means exactly what he means by those words, not in terms of the legal concept, but what he means if you using those words and how he apparently understands the word de facto authority. I fully agree with you that also in the field of criminal law, of course, that there is a distinction to be made, but I'm seeking, first of all, at this moment, to understand what the meaning is of the words used by the witness. That's what is my aim at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, clearly, I'm approaching this from the point of view of a police commander and not from the point of view of a lawyer, which I am not and never have been. I hope that, in examination-in-chief yesterday and in the report which I've submitted to the Chamber, I've explained my views on command and control, which I see as different concepts from the words I'm using in relation to influence and cooperation and things like that. And I'll try to make sure that I make that distinction, particularly in relation to Ms. Gustafson's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my understanding, when you are saying this may influence the behaviour of others, what you are apparently then saying is that the role, the words used by someone chairing a meeting may have an effect on what other people are doing. That's -- may have an effect, I say -- do not say -- have an effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me create an example. In my roles in Northern Ireland and in Kosovo, I had regular meetings with senior military personnel, and I would make quite clear to them where I thought there was a need for patrolling, where I thought there was a need for joint patrolling, or for military patrolling on its on and so on. But I couldn't say to a major-general or even to a captain, Go and patrol this area. What I would say is, Look, together this is our task, this is what we have got to achieve, this is the way I see us approaching it, how can you help? And, usually, the military would assist. And in the same way, the military would come to me and they would say, Look, from our analysis of the situation, this is where we need to be, and because the rules in force at the moment require police to accompany military patrols, can you supply a policeman to do this, please? And the answer would be, Well, if I have got a policeman, I will supply them, but I'm not talking this as an order from you, whether you're a lieutenant-general or a lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, just to get back to this issue of the daily meetings. Would you agree that what actually happened at those meetings would be more relevant to determining the nature of General Cermak's relationship with the civilian police and the extent of any de facto authority he had over them than your experience with multi-agency meetings in other contexts would be?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't dispute for one moment that direct evidence as to what took place in the meetings would have greater probative value than my experience in similar meetings elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm asking because you don't discuss anywhere in your report, as far as I can see, what actually happened at these meetings. And I'm wondering what your methodological reason is for that.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, forgive me for appearing to contradict or to contradict what seems to be implicit in the question, but I think in my references to the evidence of certain witnesses - and I can be more precise about that if necessary - there -- this is an discussion of the reaction of search witnesses to their relationship with General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could you point specifically in your report to where you reference what happened at these daily meetings? And if you need to go into private session -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well I think, if I'm going to discuss this issue more precisely, it probably would be necessary to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Madam Usher, could you escort Mr. Albiston out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have been reminded that I am addressing your oral decision that you gave just prior to the other break, and Mr. Misetic reminds me that you had ordered that that discussion should have been in private session as well. And that -- if I can refer the Chamber back to the two exhibits that Your Honour addressed at the close of the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can give you those numbers. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm aware of what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We'll have a break, and we will resume at five minutes to -- five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, I'd like to ask you a question about a statement you make in your report at paragraph 3.35, which is: "A review of witness testimony reveals that Witness 86 did not accept that General Cermak had any authority over the civilian police." Are you referring there to formal legal authority or both legal and factual authority?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. It's just -- under an abundance of caution, Your Honour, this need to be in private session, and I don't know if we are or not, or closed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is part of the public report, and questions were asked on this yesterday. So I didn't think it needed to be. But I'm in the Court's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think a reference to the witness by his pseudonym, if we do not go into any details and are just -- questions are put on the abstract level, then there seems to be no problem. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you still have my question?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I think, keeping it at the abstract, the answer is that the assessment I make this relation to that witness's evidence, I did not distinguish between those two concepts, and, in reading his testimony, it didn't seem to me that he was distinguishing between them either.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Right before the break, you referred to contradictory references in his evidence, and you stated sometimes Witness 86 ascribed a certain authority to General Cermak, and in the next sentence there is an expression which appears to resile from that. And it appears then that you have made an assessment of this evidence, in spite of contradictory references, and I'd like you to explain that, particularly in light of your earlier remark that you were not -- did not consider yourself to have the role of assessing the accuracy of witness evidence.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't have the role of assessing the accuracy of witness evidence to matters of fact, unless there were a means whereby I could compare their evidence with the documents before me. In relation to these issues, I think there are those opportunities. If I can just go back to the first part of the question, yes, the answer which I gave was an answer directed to your question, which the question, as I recall, involved quoting to go me a fairly long chunk of testimony, I think, from the witness statement of the witness concerned, and I accepted that the quotation which you had given contained a number of elements, some of which, I think, in terms of ordinary language would be considered to contradict the sentences immediately preceding or following them, and I accept that. My conclusion as to what the evidence of these witnesses means is, as I tried to intimate earlier to the Chamber based on taking their evidence and testimony in -- in the round and comparing it with other witnesses' evidence and testimony and with the documents which describe the de jure conditions in which they were operating at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could move to paragraph 3.39 of your report. Where you say: "In terms of General Cermak's coordinating function, it is evident that he was in receipt of some information from the civilian police, in relation to crimes committed." And you cite a number of documents. And I'd like to turn to one of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Which is P2650. And that's referenced at footnote 71. It how has an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now yesterday you were asked about this document and you said at page 23.790: "Yes. Well, I think we can see by looking at a combination of the English translation and the original document that this, as you say from Chief Cetina, and it's information being supplied again to the Knin garrison for the information of the garrison commander General Cermak. And it amounts to a very brief rehearsal of information, in relation to the killing of three people, and informs the General that the correct investigative and judicial procedure has been initiated." Now, your answers suggests to me, and I would like to confirm this, that you don't have any information about the circumstances that caused Mr. Cetina to sent this report to General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So what -- in light of the fact that you have cited this report as evidence of General Cermak's coordinating function, what exactly do you consider him to be coordinating here?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- this document is one of a number of documents which show General Cermak being given information about crime matters, and, therefore, I felt that it was a document upon which I would be expected to produce some observations. It's a very thin document, and it's right that I should bring it to the attention of the Court, because it connects General Cermak with crime, which is what I was asked to look at. But I don't have any background information which explains the full context of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you also cite this document in paragraph 3.71, where you is that state that: "General Cermak was passing and receiving information concerning crimes as part of his liaison role." When you refer to "liaison role" there, are you referring to his role to liaise with international organisations?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, no. I'm referring to his function of liaison been different agencies that were present in Knin at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And what specifically does this document indicate, in terms of his liaison role? What is he -- who is he liaising between here?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he is receiving a report on a crime from Mr. Cetina. On other occasions, I have been able to demonstrate why he was receiving a report on a crime, or at least to offer an interpretation to this Chamber. In relation to this one, I can't. But I thought, in the interests of completion, the document should be -- not be ignored or discarded.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But there's no indication, and you have no knowledge of him liaising between two bodies, in relation to this --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in relation to this specific matter, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to P2645.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Which is another document you cite in footnote 72 of paragraph 3.39 in relation to General Cermak's coordinating function. And, again, you were shown this yesterday, and you stated at page 23.791: "... this document is it not entirely clear to me, or should I say the purpose of the document is not entirely clear to me." And a little further down you said: "I think what is quite clear is that because of the recipients and the way that the paper is addressed, there's no expectation of any action on the part of General Cermak in response to this document." And, again, I take it that you don't have any knowledge as to why this report was written or why it was being sent to General Cermak. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am unable to link that to any other thing which seeks that information, no. I don't say it doesn't exist, I'm simply not in a position to identify or cite it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, again, you have cited that document in paragraph 3.71 as evidence that General Cermak was passing and receiving information concerning crimes as part of his liaison role. You don't have any information about -- as to whether or not he was liaising between two bodies, in relation to this particular document, do you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think, perhaps, it should be the other way around that, in relation to these documents, I'm not stating a proposition and then stating the documents to support the proposition; I'm looking at the documents and trying to offer the Chamber an interpretation of their part in this scene, this scenario.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, when you say in paragraph 3.71, at the end, you say: "I based this conclusion on witness testimony concerning meetings at which General Cermak was present and on documents which indicate that General Cermak was passing and receiving information concerning crimes as part of his liaison role." And then this is an footnote, and I understood that footnote to refer to documents that were supporting the proposition. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But then the footnote refers to a lot of other documents as well; whereas, the grouping that you were asking me about are these documents which I'm seeking to assist the Court with.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So some of the documents support the proposition and some don't. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in relation to this particular report from Mr. Gambiroza, the one dated the 21st of October, 1995. General Cermak, in one of his interviews with the Prosecution, recounted a conversation that he had with Mr. Gambiroza about the same incident that is the subject of this report. And in that interview, he said about this report or this incident, he said --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is, for the benefit of the Court and the parties, P2526, at page 82 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: "Just before winter, in October, I was with my people from logistics. We went" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, if I may inquire in what direction you are heading. Because, of course, the Chamber is familiar with the evidence in relation to, I would say, this event, the name Pasic appears, all that, the witness apparently could not give any further information as to why he used this document as a -- as an indication that it would have been sent to him as -- in order to liaise with the internationals. I'm -- I was wondering to what extent, where the witness apparently has no knowledge, which means that - well, perhaps not for -- for specific reasons, he has just put this document in the footnote - what the use of is going into the background of this report with this witness. If it is for the Chamber, the Chamber is aware of the background of this document and the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the -- the witness has relied on this report in terms of his conclusions as to General Cermak's coordinating versus commanding role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in light of the fact that he is an expert drawing conclusions, I am attempting to test those. If the Chamber isn't it -- and I was attempting to ask him to draw conclusions as to the nature of that role on the basis of this information. If the Chamber doesn't want those conclusion from this witness, I'm happy to move on. That was the end goal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- we can perhaps do that in a different way. Mr. Albiston, if there would be a background in relation to matter, which places Mr. Cermak in a role which has, I think, correct me when I'm wrong, but has got nothing to do with liaising with the internationals, but, rather, with his concern for the well-being of people in a village and perhaps his personal relationship with persons involved in this event, would there be any reason for you still to claim that this document would be indicative for his liaising role with the international organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that would be new information for me, sir, and obviously I would have to reconsider my position in the light of new information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we -- the Chamber is not assisted by inviting the witness to go look at the full background of this and then to see whether he comes to other conclusions or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I'll accept the guidance. It puts me in a difficult position, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- one could not reasonably expect anything from informing the witness about the background other than that they shed quite a different light on why Mr. Cermak may have been informed about these events. That's --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to be clear, the end goal was to ask the witness to draw conclusions as to a coordinating versus a commanding role. If the Chamber doesn't want those conclusions from this expert witness, that's fine. But ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Coordinating, I thought it was still in -- in relation to the liaising function.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I was referring to two paragraphs of the report where this was mentioned, paragraph 3.39, where this document is cited in terms of -- in support of General Cermak's coordinating function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour has already given guidance in this regard. I understand where Ms. Gustafson wishes to go. But what we will end up doing is putting to this witness something which he know nothing about, asking for his conclusions about what Mr. Cermak has described about an incident in his interview with the OTP statement. And I wonder whether this takes the matter very much further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think I'm entitled to ask the witness to draw conclusions on the evidence, I mean, that's what he is here for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- I consulted with my colleagues. The background of this event is so specific that the Chamber does not expect it to be -- or would be highly surprised if, by any way of reasoning, this event could be considered as indicative for a certain role, the roles you mentioned, coordination, or -- coordination function or the ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or the command function. The Chamber does not prevent you from addressing this specific aspect but is of the opinion that it should be the -- perhaps the last thing to do if have you time available.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I take the Court's guidance in that regard, and I move to the next point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, I would like to move, now, to paragraph 3.42 of your report. Where you state: "It should also be remembered that high level coordination in relation to problems in the Knin and surrounding areas was being effected totally outside of the Knin garrison meetings." And you go on to discuss some of the documentation regarding that high-level coordination and you conclude: "In all of this there was no role for the garrison commander." Now, I'm just -- I'd like to ask you about this conclusion, in light of the evidence that the Chamber has received, that General Cermak was affecting a coordinating role at the daily meetings that he held at the Knin garrison with the civilian police and the military police, among others. And I'm wondering, in light of that, what the significance of whether or not he's involved in communications between Mr. Lausic or Mr. Moric or other high-level communications, in light of that, daily coordination function?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The conclusion which I'm drawing from this particular set of documents is that, when it comes to the operational business on the ground, the business of dealing with the problems that existed in the Krajina, the Knin area at this time, it was the civilian police answering through a chain of command to Mr. Moric, and the military police detachments who were answering through a chain of command to Major-General Lausic, who were actually dealing with the day-to-day, the nuts and bolts, the operational response, to these problems. These are the meetings at which there are discussions about patrolling patterns, joint patrolling, check-points, joint check-points, what's happening what's, going to happen next. There's no role in any of this, according to the documents which I cite, which are fairly comprehensive, for General Cermak -- indeed, there's one document which describes a meeting where representatives of the military police and the civilian police, who have the responsibility de jure - and I would say in light of the questions that have been put, also de facto - for dealing with these problems at which Major-General Lausic says at one stage - the meeting is in Plitvice, I think it is called. Major-General Lausic says, Look, everybody that needs to be here is here to deal with these problems. But General Cermak is not there. General Cermak's deputy or representative is not there. There is no apologies for absence by General Cermak in relation to this meeting. And the -- the document -- the document is D595, and it's a note of a meeting. And these are, in my assessment, are essential documents for understanding how the Croatian state apparatus responded to crime and disorder in this area at this time. These are the people who are dealing with the problems, and General Cermak isn't one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, just to go back something you said earlier in that answer. You talk about Mr. Moric and Mr. Lausic dealing with the day-to-day, the nuts and bolts, the operational response. "These are the meetings at which there were discussions about patrolling patterns, check-points, et cetera." And you say: "There's no role for this, according to the documents, which I cite for General Cermak." It seems to that - and correct me if I'm wrong - that there's an underlying assumption here which is that these problems, these kinds of discussions about matters such as check-points and patrols, are not taking place at the daily meetings that General Cermak it holding. And if my understanding of your assumption is correct, I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... I'm not excluding the possibility that there is discussion about those matters at those meetings. What I'm saying is that the -- my interpretation of the totality of the documents is that the decisions and the responsibility for performance, these are matters which are being dealt with in these meetings, involving the civilian police and the VP.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That answers my question. Now, I would like to turn to the next part of your report, which deals with orders issued by General Cermak to the civilian police, beginning at paragraph 3.43. And you state that: "At the outset, some documents which best fit the description of orders issued by General Cermak to the civilian police were also directed to the military police." And in that paragraph, you also state that "these orders should be seen in the context of General Cermak's international point of contact role." And I'm not really sure what you mean by that statement, "seen in the context of General Cermak's international point of contact role." Is it your position that General Cermak had the authority, in fact, to issue orders to the civilian police in relation to this appointment of contact role; and, if not, what are you saying here in your report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely not. What I'm saying is that General Cermak found himself in a position, having received complaints from Brigadier Forand, for example, or, having received other information, turned to the civilian police and the military police to achieve resolution of these problems. And I think I was trying to address two different parts of indictment, and that's why there are two sections of my report which address similar issues. And so I think that this part of my report should be read in conjunction with a later part of my report, which is round about 3.71, where I discuss whether pieces of paper with the word "order" at the top can really be understood to be orders in the full sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, in this section, you haven't directly discussed other written orders issued by General Cermak to the civilian police, including P509, which you looked at yesterday, which was the order to allow civilians unhindered entry into Knin. D504, which is General Cermak's 11 October order to transfer MUP officers to another building. And D501, which is General Cermak's 10th August decision to have the MUP hand over a former hotel and adjust it to specific requirements, and instructing the headquarters administration of the Ministry of Defence and the MUP to jointly find adequate space for the accommodation of MUP personnel. And, now, none of these three orders relate to international organisations or General Cermak's international role. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are discussed in other parts of the report. I was firstly addressing, in this section, the four documents to which I refer. But I think it's right to say that the three documents, to which you've referred, do receive attention at other parts of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in terms of their tone, in -- as orders, they don't differ in any material respects from the orders General Cermak issued in relation to the missing UN equipment. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness answers the question, perhaps the question could be framed a little bit more specifically. In that question is wrapped up three different orders. And it's perhaps unfair to the witness, without pulling up the documents and looking at them, to ask such a generic question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, I did understand Ms. Gustafson to focus just on the tone to the extent that it says "orders" rather than anything else. Is that correct, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, it was actually the -- the tone -- I mean -- of course, they all say orders. It was more addressed at the commanding tone of these documents. But I take Ms. Higgins's guidance is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness would like to view again the orders or the documents you were referring to, then he will have -- he should be given an opportunity to do so. Would you like to have a look at them, Mr. Albiston?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think, Mr. President, if I'm being invited to go through the orders line by line and compare the use of language, then it would be necessary for me to look at the three orders. If this is an general proposition that these are orders and that they purport to give instructions, irrespective of whether I take a view about their legitimacy de jure, then, the answer is, Yes, we they are all documents which say order at the top and which purport to give instructions. I don't know whether that shortens the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we'll leave it to Ms. Gustafson. If she wants to explore it further, then you may be provided with the orders until we return tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If not, then Ms. Gustafson will put her next question to you. But, Ms. Gustafson, two minutes are left.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I was about to return to those written orders, so it may make sense to break now because by the time the document comes up we'll be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and you would like to deal with them in further detail. Yes, I do not know whether you have them available to you now, Mr. Albiston. If not, we will provide copies to you. Let me just scroll up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have copies of these documents in my laptop at my hotel, so I can consider them this evening, if that would help the Court tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are talking about P509, D504, and D501, if I'm not mistaken, Ms. Gustafson. Now perhaps you would prefer to write that down. So P509, D504, and D501. If would you be kind enough to have a look at them, but also not to speak about them with anyone, so as you should not speak about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given with anyone. Then we'd like to see you back tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I have access to electronic copies of these without the need to contact any other person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's understood. And we'd like to see you back tomorrow at 9.00, because we adjourn for the day, and we resume tomorrow, Thursday, 5th of November, 9.00, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 5th day of November, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
